output.title: Why reviewer training is not enough
output.body:
Reviewer training helps, but it is only one control. If the same approval rule is used again and again, the failure is often not knowledge. It is repeatable logic, data entry, fatigue, or an edge case that training by itself will not remove. Training can improve judgment; it does not change the workflow.

The practical question is simple: are the errors mostly caused by someone not knowing the rule, or by the work itself being repetitive and manually checked every time? If it is the second case, you are looking at a workflow problem, not a classroom problem.

A plain example: if an invoice or approval check always follows the same sequence, a tired reviewer can still miss one step. A rule check can catch that kind of miss. A slide deck cannot. That is not a complaint about people. It is just how late afternoons work.

At Bareni, we build around repeatable logic steps in small-business workflows, with human approval kept in place for exceptions and higher-risk decisions. That is a policy choice, not a guarantee.

Before you add more training materials, identify one recurring decision step that follows the same logic each time and note how often it appears. If it is truly repeatable, it belongs in the workflow review first.
